reading.body:
Legal AI has moved from experimentation to deployment, but the profession's defining lesson is that unverified citations invite sanctions, so verification is now the industry standard.

The six reference points span guidance, cataloguing, benchmarking, purchasing data, and academic research. The ABA sets ethics guidance, Legaltech Hub maps the tools, Vals AI benchmarks legal reasoning, ILTA records what firms actually buy, and Stanford CodeX studies the underlying informatics. Together they cover what exists, what works, and what gets deployed.

This matters for AI because legal work is high-stakes text reasoning where errors carry professional liability. Independent benchmarks and ethics opinions act as gatekeepers, not raw model capability. The data does not cover compute, power, or infrastructure costs, and it gives no adoption numbers or performance scores, so it cannot support claims about scaling constraints.

summary: Research, review, and drafting assistance are deployed at scale; sanctions for unverified citations made verification the industry lesson.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use at 43.9% in the latest period for Professional, scientific, and technical services, NAICS 54, the sector that includes legal, up slightly from 43.3% in the prior period. The question behind that figure is narrow: in the last two weeks, did this business use AI. The survey first asked it in September 2023, and the Census Bureau suppresses some values. That number describes the whole sector, not law firms on their own, so it is a ceiling rather than a measurement of legal practice specifically.

What legal AI is actually used for shows up in the vendor and research material. Stanford CodeX, a partnership between the law school and the computer science department, describes research that builds computational models of legal systems and runs an accelerated program for student teams prototyping agentic AI applications at the intersection of technology and law, alongside a hackathon and the FutureLaw 2026 conference. Legaltech Hub reports tools aimed at concrete tasks: Steno's Transcript Genius mines deposition and trial transcripts for summaries, data points, and strategic insights, and MiAI Law, built for Australian practice, combines case law research, legislative research, case summarization, contract review, and document and pleading verification.

Vendors and money cluster around platforms that connect models to a firm's own material. Legaltech Hub describes Relativity's rebrand of RelativityOne to Relativity aiR, the launch of Relativity claiR, the acquisition of document automation company Gavel, and an MCP Connector to Claude, and reports that NetDocuments is building its AI strategy around a Legal Context Graph, arguing the advantage shifts to firms that connect AI to their own documents, knowledge, and legal authorities. OpenAI's Astra for Law, built initially for Am Law 200 firms, is described as a configuration pairing its GPT-6 Astra model with legal knowledge, tools, and plugins rather than a new model. Legaltech Hub positions itself as the directory where buyers research, vendors showcase, and investors understand the marketplace, and ILTA serves as the community for legal technologists, with Epiq announcing Model Context Protocol connectors for its AI, Discover, Narrate, and Access products.

Independent measurement is thinner than vendor claims. Vals AI benchmarks legal reasoning through evaluation of models on legal research, case-law synthesis, and statutory interpretation, which this site describes as the vendor-neutral test of whether legal AI actually reasons. This site's own Legal Models page tracks the 1000 most-downloaded open legal models on the Hugging Face Hub with licence, downloads, and release date, refreshed daily. ILTA's own framing is that AI has matured rapidly since the early days of large language models. None of the cited sources report a return-on-investment figure, so there is no measured ROI evidence here to weigh.

The regulatory and ethical posture is set by the profession rather than by statute in this material. The American Bar Association's Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence has concluded its work, having focused on AI and the Profession, AI Risk Management, AI and Access to Justice, AI Governance, AI Challenges including Generative AI, and AI and Legal Education. The ABA Center for Innovation says it will continue to address AI's impact on the profession and the practice of law, including related ethical considerations, provide guidance on trustworthy and responsible development and use, and identify strategies to mitigate AI-related risks. This site's sourced points identify the ABA Center for Innovation's work, including Formal Opinion 512 on generative AI ethics, as the profession's reference point, and note that a lawsuit tracker follows the AI docket itself.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material points to a sequence rather than a verdict. Adoption across the surrounding sector is already near half of firms per the Census Bureau, the tool categories are mapped by Legaltech Hub, the purchasing record sits with ILTA, the reasoning claims can be checked against Vals AI, and the professional guidance comes from the ABA. The citation-sanction lesson and the accuracy benchmarks are the reason to test before trusting, and the ABA's emphasis on risk mitigation is the reason to document how a tool is used. What the sources do not supply is a legal-specific adoption rate or a demonstrated financial return, and neither should be inferred from what is here.

https://www.iltanet.org/.brief: ILTA, which calls itself a trusted global resource community for legal technologists, observes that AI has matured rapidly since the early days of LLMs and that its Spring Peer to Peer topics reflect this evolution. Epiq announced the availability of Model Context Protocol connectors for Epiq AI, Epiq Discover, Epiq Narrate, and Epiq Access. Litify says its ACE product now offers firm-wide AI reasoning, workflow automation, multi-step agents, and cross-platform connectivity for legal teams.

https://www.legaltechnologyhub.com/.brief: Legaltech Hub describes itself as a global directory of legal technology solutions, tools and services, serving buyers researching legal tech, vendors showcasing their products, and investors trying to understand the marketplace. Its news coverage reports that Relativity announced a series of expansions to its AI capabilities ahead of RelFest 2026 in Chicago, among them rebranding RelativityOne as Relativity aiR in September, launching Relativity claiR in August, acquiring document automation company Gavel in June, and releasing an MCP Connector to Claude or Legal in May. The page also reports that NetDocuments is building its AI strategy around a Legal Context Graph launched in May, alongside a new benchmark and two AI features, with the company arguing that as models and tools become more interchangeable the advantage shifts to firms connecting AI to their own documents, knowledge and legal authorities. According to the page, OpenAI has released Astra for Law, built initially for Am Law 200 firms, which pairs its most recent GPT-6 Astra model with legal-specific knowledge, tools and ecosystem plugins rather than being a new model. It further notes interviews about Steno's Transcript Genius, a deposition transcript analysis tool, with vice president of product James Ehlers, and about the Australian platform MiAI Law with founder and CEO Laina Chan.

https://law.stanford.edu/codex-the-stanf.brief: CodeX is a partnership between Stanford Law School and the Department of Computer Science that studies how information technology can improve legal processes. It applies data science and artificial intelligence to build quantitative and predictive models of the law, moving beyond traditional empirical analysis. The program offers a hands-on accelerated track for interdisciplinary student teams to prototype Agentic AI and the CFAA applications at the intersection of technology and law. CodeX also hosts a hackathon that brings together AI innovators, machine learning specialists, and legal professionals to prototype future legal technology. Additionally, it organizes an international conference and FutureLaw 2026 to bring together leaders in law, technology, and policy to discuss sustainable, ethical, and responsible AI in legal systems.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The World of AI catalogues what it calls the 1000 most-downloaded open legal models on the Hugging Face Hub, listing each one's licence, download count and release date. It says the catalogue is rebuilt daily from the Hub's public API, sorted by all-time downloads, with every model linking to its own Hub page. The page records its last verification date as 2026-09-28. It also advertises books and consulting services, and describes the wider site as an atlas of what the law says, who is suing whom and what the words mean, rebuilt daily from primary sources.

https://www.americanbar.org/groups/cente.brief: The Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence has finished its work, and the Center for Innovation will keep addressing how AI affects the legal profession, including ethical issues, trustworthy development, and risk-mitigation strategies. It will also provide guidance on responsible AI use. Past webinars from the Task Force examine how AI is reshaping law practice, covering practical applications, new legal technology, and the ethical, professional-responsibility, and regulatory challenges lawyers must navigate.
